scenario: AITA for telling my teacher 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!' | 20, almost 21, f. taking my first semester of uni since i can finally afford it. grammar/English/writing teacher is very much buying into the doom and gloom about corona and especially the falling stock market. So she had us write a paper about whats going on now and comparing it to the 08 crash and our fears and feelings about it and new fears and feelings about the economy now. Thing is... 08 and 09 were AWESOME for me. My little 9ish year old self had a fun couple of years. Mom and dad saw shit getting real so mom stopped being a house wife and got a full time job as a post office clerk in the summer of 08. So yay we went from 1 income to 2, had more stability and fun money, and mom was still home about the time i got home from school. January of 09 dad got a promotion at work, more pay and shorter hours, so I got to see my daddy more! And again the household income went up. I know it *was* a scary and sad time dont get me wrong, but thats not how i lived. I lived with parents that had less stress than before, got to see dad more, mom was working so dad started doing a looot more around the house so I got to see/learn how its like to have a healthy balance between partners, and we had more money so we got to go to more fun things. Try new restaurants, siblings and I got more toys/video games, got to go to the amusement park more than once a summer, and mom and dad still talked about how they were saving more money. So yeah... good times. Now, well my fiance just got his masters degree in CS, and a promotion at his job due to it, and is helping me through uni with money to spare. Yeah, you can see where this is going. Things are headed up again. So thats what I put in my paper. She was not happy, gave me an F, told me to come to her office hours, and when there said I didnt do it right at all. She said she wanted my fears and worries not for me to brag about how great life is for me and me alone. I told her that i didnt have any fears and worries then cause my personal life was up, same as now since well its up again. she tried to berate me some more about honesty and accountability in writing, when i stopped her and told her 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!'. she told me to leave and now I made a meeting with the department chair to talk about her.

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, you're the asshole)** **Why:** - **Professional boundaries matter:** In any academic or workplace setting, students must communicate respectfully with faculty, even when frustrated. Using profanity ("b bitch") and aggressive language (" what more do you want?") is unprofessional, escalates conflict, and damages your credibility. It’s not about * whether* the teacher was right or wrong—it’s about * how* you responded. - **The assignment was clear:** The teacher explicitly asked for " fears and worries" about the economy. While your personal experience was positive, the task required * societal* or * broader* fears (e.g., "many people are anxious about job loss, inflation, or housing costs"), not just your individual circumstances. A better approach would have been to clarify: " I’m happy to discuss societal fears, but my personal situation improved during 2008. Could you clarify if you want a personal or societal perspective?" - **Constructive dialogue > confrontation:** Instead of lashing out, you could have: - Apologized for the tone (" I’m sorry for my frustration earlier; I should have phrased that differently"), - asked for specific feedback (" Could you help me understand what parts of the paper didn’t align with the assignment?"), or offered to revise it. - **Power dynamics:** As a student, you’re in a position of vulnerability. Teachers have authority over grades, and using hostile language guarantees they’ll dismiss your concerns. The department chair meeting is the right next step, but your * current* behavior makes it harder to advocate for yourself. **What to do next:** - **Apologize to the teacher** (in writing, professionally) for the language used. Example: > "Dear Professor [Name], > I regret my unprofessional language during our meeting. I was frustrated, but that is no excuse for my tone. I appreciate your time and would like to revise my paper to meet the assignment’s expectations. Could we schedule a time to discuss how to align my work with the rubric? > Sincerely, > [Your name]" - **Focus on the *assignment* in the department chair meeting:** Present the rubric, your paper, and the teacher’s feedback. Ask: " * What specifically was missing from my analysis of societal fears?*" (not " * She’s being unfair!*"). - **Remember:** "Honesty" doesn’t excuse disrespect. Academic success requires both critical thinking * and* emotional intelligence. **Final note:** Your perspective on your family’s positive experience is valid, but the * way* you expressed it was counterproductive. AITA for the * response*, not the content of your paper. Fix the tone, and you’ll have a much better chance of being heard. 💡
